Madam Chair, this committee must provide political direction to accelerate the achievement of the SDGs. Thank you, Ambassador, for your statement. Now I would like to invite the distinguished representative of Croatia to take the floor.

As we move closer to 2030, the pace and scale of SDG implementation must accelerate. This demands financing approaches that mobilize long-term resources, strengthen national ownership, and ensure that the UN system delivers with greater impact on the ground. Streamline the debates, a realistic submission deadline, strengthen text based consultations and improve documentation can significantly enhance efficiency and predictability. These reforms matter because they directly strengthen the link between the committee's decisions and operational activities for development on the ground. Clearer mandates. More concise resolutions and better coordination help UN country teams deliver more coherent, integrated support aligned with national priorities. Croatia is proud to support mandate discipline and efforts to make resolutions more action-oriented and aligned with the 2030 Agenda. These reforms improve financing outcomes by reducing duplication, improving coherence, and enabling more strategic resource allocation. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Croatia. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Singapore.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Singapore congratulates you and the members of the Bureau on your election. You have our full support. Four years remain to deliver the 2030 Agenda, but the world we find ourselves in, it is not the one in which we set out the Sustainable Development Goals. Trade is fragmenting, the cost of capital has risen, Official development assistance has dropped sharply, and too many developing countries now spend more on debt servicing than on healthcare or education. We do not lack solutions, nor do we lack capital. Our challenge is ensuring that the solutions and capital reach the places that need it most, at a cost they can afford. Singapore would highlight three priorities. First, we must make public money work harder. Public finance, including ODA and concessional finance, remains indispensable, but every public dollar must be deployed to draw in several more by absorbing risks that investors cannot yet price, building pipelines of bankable projects, and by giving investors the policy predictability and confidence they need to commit for the long term. The severe commitment already sets out the agenda; what remains is implementation. Singapore has already put into action catalytic instruments such as our Financing Asia's Transition Partnership, FAST-P blended finance facility, which aims to mobilize up to US$5 billion in collaboration with public, private, and philanthropic sector partners to de-risk and finance green and transition projects in Asia. Second, digital technologies and artificial intelligence in particular will only advance development if it reaches the last mile. Much of the global conversation on AI centers on the large and frontier models. For many developing countries, a more useful question might perhaps be what smaller, targeted AI models and solutions can do, models trained on local languages and data, able to run on modest infrastructure, and built to solve specific problems for a farmer, a clinic, or a small manufacturer. Such tools can lower transaction costs, improve access to finance and public services, and make small firms visible to lenders who cannot yet assess the risk. Singapore will continue to work with our partners to make our AI models accessible and offer practical solutions for local conditions. Third, we must start the conversation on what comes after 2030 now, not in 2029. The SDGs have given the international community a common language for sustainable development. that is worth keeping. But we should be candid on two counts. First, measurement is lacking. Too many targets still cannot be assessed for lack of data. Investing in national statistical systems provides us with high return on spending. Second, focus is lacking. The SDGs are integrated, and that is precisely why some investments in energy access, digital connectivity and education have such a multiplier effect. When official resources are shrinking, trying to do everything everywhere all at once spreads them too thinly to make a real difference. Capital should go where it catalyzes most, guided by each country's priorities and comparative advantages. We must begin this discussion in earnest ahead of the 2027 SDG Summit, including during this Main Committee session. Madam Chair, Singapore will continue contributing through partnerships, innovation and capacity building. We should use the remaining years to accelerate what works, while also preparing the foundations for sustainable development beyond 2030. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Poland and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Senegal.

Thank you, Madam Chair, Excellencies, Distinguished representatives, many. The theme for this year is particularly important and should give us all pause. Less than four years from the final date of the 2030 Agenda, the international community must face more than ever up to urgent, complex and interconnected challenges. The fruits of economic growth remain fragile and unequally shared. The economies of developing countries are facing structural obstacles that get in the way of sustainable growth, industrialization, the implementation of viable infrastructure, job creation and resilience to climate change. According to the most recent estimates of the World Bank, Around 464 million Africans were living in extreme poverty, monetary poverty in 2024. If we take into account the multidimensional poverty index, the number of people concerned rises significantly. It's 593 million Africans. These difficulties are exacerbated by many internal and external factors, including the historic decrease in official development assistance. According to the OECD, ODA fell by 23.1% in 2025 and was only 0.26% of the combined GDP of the member states and associate states of the Development Assistance Committee. It is our responsibility to promote sustainable and inclusive development. That calls for not just coherent, suitable and ambitious measures, but also at the national level and the international level. On the national level, We must significantly improve the mobilization of internal resources through, among other things, the modernization of the tax system, the enlargement of the tax base, and the progressive integration of the informal sector into the tax system through simplified regimes. The desired modernization could be brought about through the digitalization of the tax administration by giving the physical physical and legal persons concerned, the elements to make their declarations and payments electronically. In Senegal, the reforms needed are implemented through the Centax system. That's an online system of the General Directorate of Taxes and Remains, which allows taxpayers to report and pay their taxes in all security. The efficient mobilization of internal resources also requires an improvement in governance and to fight more effectively against illicit financial flows. money laundering, tax fraud, corruption, and the deviation of public funds. To meet these challenges, our legislative and regulatory mechanism in Senegal is based on the national self, the treatment of international financial information, the national counter fraud and corruption office, and the financial judicial pool. The progress made by Senegal meant that it was withdrawn or taken off the list of jurisdictions under enhanced surveillance on 24th October 2024. On the international level, it's also necessary to provide the relevant solutions to mobilize concessional financing and private capital, including through multilateral development banks and mixed financing. It's also important to implement the reform of the international financial architecture through particular attention to the representation of developing countries in decision-making bodies. In any case, the Seville commitment has set a clear and coherent framework which corresponds to the legitimate aspirations of developing countries. We must collectively enhance international cooperation, bring together strategic partnerships, but also make best use in a responsible way of science, technology and innovation with a view to resetting the world's economic trajectory and put it resolutely into the prospect of inclusive and shared prosperity. Thank you very much.
Thank you, distinguished representative of Senegal, for the statement. And now I'd like to invite the permanent representative of Namibia to take the floor. Ambassador, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Mr. President. Excellencies, Namibia congratulates you and the Bureau on your election and assures you of our full support and cooperation. We align ourselves with the statements delivered on behalf of the G77 and China and the African group. We convene at a pivotal moment where the world grapples with unprecedented challenges, from economic shocks to environmental degradation, from social inequalities to geopolitical tensions. In this context, it is in this context that we gather under the theme, financing sustainable development in a changing global economy to accelerate SDG implementation. This theme is not just timely, but necessary. It challenges us all to forge a path that is inclusive, sustainable, and adaptable to the constantly evolving global landscape. Chair, the Pact for the Future provides the framework for stronger global cooperation and collective action towards addressing today's challenges, particularly the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals, and further reinforced our commitment to multilateralism. At the core of this effort is a recognition that global transformation is not just a goal, but a necessity. This is not merely about rebuilding trust in multilateralism, but it is about recognizing one another as equal partners in the fight against poverty, inequality, and injustice. Namibia has made considerable efforts in mobilizing domestic resources. We collect roughly a third of our gross domestic product in revenue. Yet our fiscal deficit remains significant and public debt is approaching 70% of the GDP. Our experience demonstrates a simple point. Domestic resource mobilization is indispensable, but it cannot on its own close development financing gap. In July 2025, Namibia was reclassified by the World Bank from upper middle income to lower middle income country status, reflecting slower growth and revised population estimates following our census. Yet, the change in classification did not change the underlying financing realities we face. Access to affordable developing finance remains a challenge. Our experience reinforces a wider point. Access to development finance should reflect the realities countries face, rather than income per capita alone. Vulnerability, inequality, and exposure to climate shocks must also form part of that assessment. We therefore encourage international financial institutions to consider a multilateral, multidimensional vulnerability index alongside gross national income per capita, as per the General Assembly's decision in its resolution 78/322. Furthermore, financing is also about what a country can earn. Namibia introduced restrictions on the export of certain unpossessed critical minerals in 2023 to encourage domestic value addition. Countries must be able to deliver, to derive greater value from their resources, create jobs and strengthen their productive capacity. In 2024, global debt reached $102 trillion. Developing countries paid a record $921 billion in net interest that year. 61 of them now spend at least a tenth of the government revenue in interest alone. And 3.4 billion people live in countries that spend more on interest than on health and education. UNCTAD reports that since 2020, developing countries have borrowed at rates two or four times those available to the United States. In this regard, Namibia supports the UN framework, including the Borrower's Platform and the Sevilla Commitment on debt reduction. Finally, Madam Chair, the test of this session is not how many resolutions we adopt. It is whether our decisions improve the price and availability of finance for the countries that need it most. I thank you.

Finance more of their own development.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Madam Chair, Belize congratulates you and the Bureau and assure you of our support. We align ourselves with the statement delivered on behalf of the Group of 77 and China, CARICOM, and the Alliance of Small Island States. With four years remaining to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, implementation must command our attention. The commitments we have adopted must translate into affordable financing, stronger national institutions, and tangible benefits for our people. As a small island developing state, Belize faces structural vulnerabilities that income per capita alone cannot adequately capture. Climate impacts, exposure to external economic shocks, and high cost of resilient infrastructure places persistent demands on small economy. Chair, the Seville Commitment offers an opportunity to address the financing constraints that impede sustainable development. Belize calls for affordable, long-term finance, greater grant and highly concessional resources, and simpler access procedures. We note with concern the significant decline in official development assistance. Therefore, development partners must reverse this trend and honor their commitments. The Abbas for SIDS provides a clear framework for resilient prosperity. Its implementation must be embedded in UN cooperation frameworks, the development partners programs, and country strategies of the IFIs. Belize calls for sustained support for the SIDS Center of Excellence, including practical assistance with data, project preparation, and investment and debt sustainability. The MVI must inform access to concessional finance, allocations, and financing terms. Belize's access to the IDA financing under the expanded small states exceptions demonstrates that eligibility frameworks can reflect vulnerability. This approach should inform wider reform. Repeated borrowing for disaster recovery reduces resources for prevention and development. I thank the distinguished representative of Belize and invite to take the floor the distinguished delegate of the United States.

Thank you, Madam Chair. During the previous session, The Gambia and this Committee's Bureau led the Second Committee through a long overdue reckoning. Through the passage of the decision on revitalization of the work of the Second Committee, this Committee has proven that institutional reform is possible. We strongly urge all the other committees from first to sixth to look to the second committee and follow this lead in eliminating waste. But now comes the real test. We must ensure these efforts were not in vain. We're at the starting line, not the finish line. The United States strongly supports continued common-sense reforms that prioritize efficiency, accountability, and good stewardship of resources. For too long, the UN has drifted from its core mission, bogged down by a culture that prioritizes process over performance, paperwork over real-world economic results. The second committee has become a factory for zombie resolutions that reflect outdated economic paradigms and risk infringing upon national sovereignty. Business as usual is a luxury this institution can no longer afford. Moving forward, this committee must enforce efficiency across four non-negotiable pillars. First, radical consolidation. This committee must end duplicative mandates that belong elsewhere, leave technical work to specialized agencies in Rome, Geneva, and Nairobi, and merge fragmented resolutions into lean omnibus frameworks. Second, end the annual machine. The committee must shift stable items to multi-year reviews. This is needed to break the cycle of the perpetual drafting machine. Third, text streamlining. The committee must enforce hard page limits, strip repetitive preambular clauses, and move historical references older than five years into footnotes. We're not historians. We're here to deliver measurable results. And fourth, stop mandate creep. Each resolution must fall into this committee's core mandate on economic and financial issues. But this mandate has its limits. The UN must stop playing shadow regulator and respect the independent governance of the World Trade Organization, international financial institutions like the World Bank and IMF, and sovereign national regulatory bodies. These four pillars are not mere suggestions. They will define our engagement in this session. During the session, the United States will engage selectively on resolutions, and we encourage others to do the same. Member states should not feel pressured to engage or rubber stamp every resolution raised in the session. We will continue to oppose resolutions that promote social engineering, push divisive political or social issues, or infringe on sovereignty. We will oppose resolutions that position this Committee as an administrative delivery mechanism for central planning or top-down global development targets. Decades of government-to-government aid have often produced dependency, inefficiency, and corruption, rather than lasting prosperity. As Secretary Rubio has stated, we must prioritize trade over aid, opportunity over dependency, and investment over assistance. Real human flourishing comes from sovereign nations mobilizing their own resources, establishing the rule of law, protecting intellectual and physical property rights, and creating pro-growth, free market environments. It is private business that builds successful economies, not U.N. decrees. Expanding trade opportunities is a proven pathway to prosperity. By fostering fair and reciprocal trade relationships, we empower nations to attract investment, create jobs, and unlock private sector-led growth. In short, the Second Committee must pivot from managing dependency to fostering dynamism. The United States stands ready to work with delegations that seek to unlock private capital, champion innovation, and empower entrepreneurs. Madam Chair, colleagues, we look forward to working with you in the weeks ahead.

I thank you.

Tajikistan is looking forward to working with all delegation in advancing the work of the second committee during the 81st session. Thank you.

Strengthening domestic resource mobilization remains key. At the same time, official development assistance retains its distinctive and catalytic role, particularly for least developed countries and fragile contexts. Greece remains concerned about the current decline in ODA. We should ensure that scarce concessional resources reach those most in need while supporting domestic capacities, strengthening institutions, and leveraging additional sustainable investment. Second, we need to mobilize sustainable investment at greater scale. Multilateral development banks and development finance institutions are key to expanding access to affordable long-term finance, sharing risks, and mobilizing responsible private capital. In this context, the EU's Global Gateway represents an important contribution. Through a team Europe approach, it seeks a mo- it seeks to mobilize public and private resources to help bridge the global investment gap and build mutually beneficial partnerships based on local ownership and partner countries' priorities. Third, we need stronger action on debt and the cost of capital. We should continue to support partner countries in their efforts to strengthen debt sustainability and reduce borrowing costs, including through sound public financial management. Fourth, financing must build resilience and productive capacity. In an increasingly shock-prone world, development financing should enable countries not only to respond to crisis, but also to build greater resilience for the future. Investment in climate and disaster resilience and greater economic diversification are essential. Developing countries must also be supported in harnessing the transformations shaping the global economy, including the green and digital transitions and artificial intelligence. Fifth, multilateral cooperation remains indispensable. Greece remains fully committed to strengthen multilateral cooperation and the rules-based international order. The international financial architecture must continue to evolve and become more inclusive, representative, and effective, while strengthening the voice of developing countries and improving their access to affordable and predictable financing. Madam Chair, as we accelerate SDG implementation, we should also begin thinking about the era beyond 2030. But this discussion must not divert attention or resources from commitments already made.

As we.

Look towards the 2027 SDG Summit, our immediate task is clear, to translate commitments into concrete action, strengthen international cooperation.

I thank you.

In closing, Ireland looks forward to working together with all of you over the coming weeks to agree meaningful outcomes and advance our shared aim to deliver a more sustainable, equitable and resilient future for all. Madam Chair, the delegation of Burkina Faso congratulates you and the members of the Bureau on your election. Burkina Faso aligns itself with the statements made by the G77 and China, by the Group of African States, and by the group of the least developed countries. The theme of the general debate, financing sustainable development in a changing global economy to accelerate implementation of the sustainable development goals, is of particular importance. Just four years from the deadline, the SDGs remain out of reach for a good number of countries. That's because the development momentum is heavily blunted by the combination of security crises, climate crises, sanitary crises, terrorism, geopolitical tensions, over-indebtedness, the decrease in development financing, and the crisis of multilateralism. How can we achieve the SDGs when some states are financing and arming terrorist groups who destabilize our countries and compromise the implementation of our development programs? In that context, the financing of development is becoming a major issue. Because the international financial architecture is showing its limitations with regard to the needs of developing economies, we must rethink our approaches, reduce our dependence on external financing, and enhance our own development mechanisms. Therefore, Madam Chair, in Burkina Faso, under the leadership of Captain Ibrahim Traore, President of Burkina Faso, the country now has a relaunch plan for 2026 to 2030, which aims to make Burkina Faso a sovereign and prosperous nation on the basis of sustainable, endogenous development. This plan aims in particular to enhance the mobilization of internal resources with the aim of covering 63.9% of financing needs, while promoting the national potential and developing innovative mechanisms such as people's shareholding, green financing and public-private partnerships. So far, there's no ambiguity about the results. The concrete progress has been made. Food security has been enhanced. Health, education, hydraulic energy and digital infrastructure is developing, while the local processing of raw materials is creating more added value and jobs. The people and diaspora of Guinea-Bissau have fully supported this view and are contributing to the financing of many national projects. This experience shows that in a world economy in flux, innovative mechanisms for mobilizing resources can help to finance development. Their success, however, depends on people's trust and confidence, the transparency of resource management, and the relevance of the projects that are financed. My delegation also invites the international community to favor indigenous solutions in a spirit of mutual respect, solidarity, and true partnership. That is how the SDGs will be fully achieved.
